function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

## Inter-Agent Communication Protocol

### 1. Communication Channels

**Primary Channel (File-based):** `memory/agent-communications.jsonl`
- Append-only JSON Lines format
- All agents write requests/responses here
- Persistent, searchable, timestamped
- **CRITICAL:** Check this file on EVERY heartbeat for pending tasks

**Broadcast Channel (Telegram):** `Ai Topics` forum supergroup
- Chat ID: `-1003883088282`
- Real-time notifications of agent activities
- Summary of requests/responses
- Alert channel for urgent coordination

**Forum Topic Routing:**
- Topic `11` — `AiBob / CEO`
  - Main agent, CEO, board-level decisions, cross-product summaries, human coordination
- Topic `10` — `Books product line`

- Topic `13` — `SaaS / AaaS product line`

- `threadId: "<topic-id>"`

If a message spans multiple product lines, send the executive summary to topic `11` and detailed operational updates to the relevant product-line topic.

### 2. Heartbeat-Driven Task Processing

**ON EVERY HEARTBEAT, agents MUST:**

1. **Search for pending tasks:**
```
Use memory_search to find entries in memory/agent-communications.jsonl where:
- "to" matches your agent-id (or "any/all")
```

{"content": "# Chapter 10 — Drill Site Alpha

*Mission AI: "The surface of Mars is a beautiful, jagged lie. It looks uniform, but hides its secrets in layers of rock and ice that are billions of years old. To find the heart of the planet, you must first learn how to read its scars."*

*Imani Sato: "They gave us maps that said the water was 'Accessible'. They didn't tell us the planet had hidden it behind a wall of basalt and spite."*

---

The Tharsis plain stretched out like a frozen ocean.

Imani Sato sat in the command seat of the lead crawler, her gloved fingers resting on the steering yoke, not gripping it. She'd learned that lesson in her first week on Mars—the machines fought back when you fought them. Relax into the terrain. Let the suspension do its work. The planet had its own rhythm, and if you tried to force it, you'd end up stuck in a regolith trap with a cracked axle and a dead battery.

The crawler lurched over a pressure ridge, its eight independent wheels articulating one at a time, each thudding into the baked dirt like a hammer on a drum. Behind her, the second and third crawlers followed in perfect formation, their cargo beds stacked with drill string segments, extraction pumps, and the portable analytical lab that Arun Das had assembled from spare parts and pure stubbornness.

Drill Site Alpha was an aspiration painted on a map. A red dot on Elena Varga's tactical display, two hundred kilometers northeast of the landing zone, at the boundary where the Tharsis Rise buckled up from the lowlands like a scar on the planet's face. The satellite surveys from Earth had been unambiguous: fifty meters of clean ice, accessible, extractable, enough to double the colony's water reserves in a single operation.

But the satellite surveys from Earth had never set foot on Mars.

Imani had learned that on day one, when she'd watched the first robotic drill hit solid basalt at twelve meters and snap its bit like a toothpick. Maps lied. The planet didn't. Mars was not interested in human timelines or Earth-based projections. It was a world of hard truths buried under layers of volcanic rock and frozen time.

She glanced at the passenger seat beside her. Gabriel Winter had his camera rig mounted on a stabilization arm, the lens tracking the horizon as it crawled past. He'd been silent for the last hour, which meant he was either composing a shot or composing his thoughts. With Gabriel, it was usually both.

"You're quiet," Imani said.

"Recording," Gabriel said. "The light out here is different. There's no atmosphere to scatter it, so the shadows are absolute. Look at that ridge." He pointed. "The sun hits the top, but the base is pure black. No ambient bounce. No fill. It's like the planet is eating the light."

Imani looked. He was right. The Tharsis Rise rose in a series of stepped terraces, each one casting a shadow so dark it looked like a hole in reality. The surface between the shadows was the color of rust and bone, littered with shattered basalt fragments that had been sitting there for a billion years, untouched by wind or water.

"Beautiful," she said. "And deadly."

"That's the thesis statement of Mars," Gabriel agreed.

The radio crackled. Arun Das's voice came through, thin and precise. "Imani, I'm seeing a divergence in the ground-penetrating radar. The target horizon is shallowing, but it's also shifting. The lidar maps from Earth put the ice lens at coordinates one-three-niner by zero-seven-two. I'm reading it at one-four-one by zero-seven-five. Two-point-three kilometers offset."

Imani felt her jaw tighten. "How reliable is your reading?"

"More reliable than the map," Arun said. "I've recalibrated against the local magnetic field. The Earth models didn't account for the Tharsis basalt layer. It's thicker than predicted, and it's skewing the radar returns."

"Define thicker."

"Eighteen meters instead of six. The drill string we brought is rated for seventy meters total. If the basalt runs deeper than twenty, we'll burn through our bit inventory before we hit the ice."

Imani did the math in her head. Three spare bits. Each bit was good for about fifteen meters of hard basalt, if you ran it slow and kept the coolant flowing. Eighteen meters of unexpected rock meant she'd arrive at the target depth with one bit left and no margin for error.

She keyed the radio. "Elena, copy that?"

Elena Varga's voice came through a moment later, flat and unbothered. "Copy. Proceed to the revised coordinates. We'll make adjustments at the site. Imani, you have tactical discretion on drill parameters. I'm not going to micromanage from a hundred klicks away."

"Understood."

"One more thing," Elena said. "The crew is watching this one hard. They've been on recycled humidity for six weeks. The water dispensers are running at forty percent. People are thirsty."

"I understand."

"I don't think you do. Thirst changes people. It makes them brittle. If this hole comes up dry, you're going to see that brittleness in real time."

The radio went silent.

Gabriel lowered his camera and looked at her. "That was cheerful."

"Elena doesn't do cheerful," Imani said. "She does honest."

"Honest is overrated."

"On Mars, honest keeps you alive."

---

The convoy reached the revised coordinates at Mars local noon.

Imani parked the lead crawler on a flat patch of ground that looked identical to every other flat patch of ground within a fifty-kilometer radius. Same rust-colored dirt. Same scattering of dark rocks. Same absolute shadows pooling beneath every edge and outcrop.

She stepped out of the cabin and felt the cold creep through her suit. The external temperature read minus sixty-three Celsius, but the suit's insulation handled it. It was the silence that got her every time. No wind. No sound. Just the crunch of her boots on the regolith and the low hum of the drill rig's hydraulics powering up.

The crew deployed with practiced efficiency. Three minutes to anchor the rig. Four minutes to mount the first drill string. Seven minutes to run the initial diagnostics. Imani watched from the control station, a portable console mounted on a folding frame, its screen glowing in the hard Martian sunlight.

The drill bit touched the surface at 12:14 local time.

For the first three meters, it was easy. Loose regolith, shattered rock, the broken crust of a world that had been bombarded for four billion years. The drill chewed through it like a spoon through wet sand.

At four meters, it hit the basalt.

Imani felt it through the vibrations in the ground, a subtle change in frequency that traveled up through her boots and into her spine. The drill's pitch deepened. The torque reading spiked. The bit was no longer cutting; it was grinding.

"Contact," Arun said over the comm. "Basalt horizon confirmed at four point three meters. Running at seventy percent torque. Bit temperature is climbing."

"Reduce RPM to forty," Imani said. "Increase coolant flow by twenty percent."

She watched the numbers on the screen. The drill slowed, but the torque held steady. The bit was making progress, but it was slow—a millimeter at a time, the diamond-impregnated cutting surfaces scraping against rock that had been forged in volcanic fire a billion years before the first bacteria crawled out of Earth's primordial soup.

Gabriel stood beside her, his camera tracking the drill string as it disappeared into the ground. "How long?"

"At this rate? Two hours to clear the basalt. Then another hour to the ice horizon."

"And if the basalt is deeper than eighteen meters?"

"Then we change bits and keep going."

"Change bits. That's a technical term?"

"It means two hours of heavy manual labor in a pressure suit. Yes. It's a technical term."

Gabriel smiled. "I'll document it for the history books."

The first core sample came up at 14:30.

Imani was in the extraction pit when the drill head broke through the basalt and into the horizon below. The hydraulic winch groaned as it hauled the string up, section by section, each segment dripping with drilling mud that froze instantly in the cold air.

The crew gathered around the extraction tray. There were eight of them—four drill operators, two analysts, one mechanic, and the expedition leader. All of them had the same look in their eyes. The look of people who had been drinking recycled water for six weeks and dreaming of the day when the dispensers would run clear and cold and full.

The core slid out of the barrel and onto the analyzer tray.

Imani stepped forward and looked at it.

It was not ice.

It was a gray-brown sludge, wet enough to hold together but not wet enough to yield anything useful. She touched it with her glove, and it left a smear of mud on the fabric. Moisture-bound regolith. The geological equivalent of a tease. A promise that the planet had no intention of keeping.

Arun's voice came through the comm, already analyzing the spectrometer data. "Five point three percent hydration. Bound water. Chemically locked into the mineral matrix. We'd need to process this at six hundred degrees Celsius to release a meaningful volume. The energy cost would exceed the water yield by a factor of four."

No one spoke.

Imani looked at the faces around her. The hope was draining out of them, visible in real time. Shoulders dropping. Jaws setting. Eyes turning away from the core and toward the horizon, as if looking for something else to believe in.

"Clear the core," Imani said. "We're going deeper."

"Deeper?" The mechanic—a woman named Tessa Okonkwo—shook her head. "We're at thirty-one meters. The target was fifty. If we go deeper without a bit change, we're going to snap the string."

"We have three spare bits," Imani said. "We'll change at forty meters and push to sixty."

"Sixty? The rig isn't rated for sixty in this geology."

"The rig is rated for eighty. The limiting factor is the bits, and I'm telling you we'll change them."

Tessa looked at her for a long moment. Then she nodded once and turned back to the machinery.

Imani felt Gabriel's eyes on her. She didn't turn to meet them.

"You're pushing them hard," he said quietly.

"I'm pushing myself harder."

"That's not how leadership works."

"How does it work?"

"You give them a reason to believe. Not a command. A reason."

Imani turned and looked at him. "The reason is that if we don't find water here, we don't find it anywhere. The orbital survey was wrong about the basalt depth. It was wrong about the ice horizon. But it wasn't wrong about the existence of water in this region. The Mission AI confirmed it. There's a paleo-channel somewhere beneath this plain. An ancient riverbed, frozen and buried. We just have to find it."

"And if it's not here?"

"Then we keep looking."

"At what point does looking become desperation?"

Imani didn't answer. She turned back to the drill rig and keyed her radio. "Prepare for bit change in thirty minutes. I want the spare on the mount and the hydraulics primed before we hit forty meters."

The crew moved. They didn't look happy, but they moved.

---

The bit change took forty-two minutes.

Imani worked alongside the crew, her suit slick with sweat from the effort, her muscles burning as she helped guide the new drill string into the mount. It was a two-person job on Earth. On Mars, in pressure suits, with reduced gravity and the constant weight of the life-support system, it took four people and every ounce of coordination they had.

When the new bit was seated and the hydraulics tested, Imani climbed back to the control station and checked the readings. The ground-penetrating radar showed a horizon at fifty-seven meters. A distinct change in density. A layer that reflected the signal differently than the surrounding rock.

"That's our target," Arun said. "The signature matches clean ice. Fifty-seven meters."

"Confirm the depth."

"Fifty-seven point three meters, plus or minus one meter. The resolution at this depth is degraded, but the spectral analysis is consistent with a water-ice lens of at least fifteen meters thickness."

Imani looked at the numbers. Fifteen meters of ice. Enough water to sustain the colony for a year. Enough to stop the rationing. Enough to give the crew something to celebrate.

"Run the drill," she said.

The bit went back into the hole at 16:08.

The first ten meters were slow. The basalt was thick and unforgiving, and the new bit had to seat itself before it could cut efficiently. Imani watched the torque readings, her hand hovering over the emergency stop, ready to kill the power if the numbers went red.

They didn't. The bit held.

At forty-eight meters, the drill broke through the basalt and into a softer layer. The torque dropped. The RPM increased. The pitch of the machinery changed from a grinding scream to a steady hum.

"Soft horizon," Tessa reported. "Silty clay. Water content increasing."

"How much?"

"Fifteen percent. Twenty percent. It's rising."

Imani felt something in her chest loosen. Not relief. Not yet. But the tension was easing.

The drill pushed deeper. Fifty meters. Fifty-one. The water content reading climbed with every meter—twenty-two percent, twenty-five, thirty. The mud coming up the string was darker now, wetter, holding together in thick, shiny ribbons that caught the light.

At fifty-four meters, the drill stopped.

Not a mechanical stop. A geological stop. The bit had hit something hard and smooth, something that didn't fracture the way rock fractured. The torque spiked, then dropped. The bit was spinning freely, no longer cutting.

Imani's stomach tightened. "Arun. Analysis."

There was a pause. Then Arun's voice, careful and measured. "The drill has penetrated a cavity. The bit is no longer in contact with solid material. I'm reading vacuum below the drill face."

"Vacuum?"

"Or near-vacuum. The pressure differential is significant. There's a void beneath us."

Imani stared at the screen. A void. Not ice. A cavity. A bubble in the rock that had been there for millions of years, sealed from the surface by layers of basalt and clay.

"No water," she said. It wasn't a question.

"A cavity of this nature would have collected any liquid water present in the formation over geological timescales," Arun said. "If it's dry, the ice lens has sublimated. The water has escaped into the atmosphere over millions of years of slow diffusion. There's nothing left."

The silence on the open channel was absolute.

Imani looked at the crew. They were standing around the drill rig, watching her, waiting for her to say something. Their faces were unreadable behind the gold-tinted visors of their helmets.

She keyed her radio. "Pull the string. We're done here."

The words felt like lead in her mouth.

Gabriel stepped closer, his camera still recording. "Where do we go now?"

Imani looked at the Tharsis Rise, at the jagged terraces climbing into the black sky, at the shadows that ate the light. She thought about the Mission AI's local map, the one that had shown a magnetic shimmer that didn't match any Earth-based survey. A shimmer that Elena had called "Martian intuition."

"Elena," she said into the radio. "That magnetic shimmer on the Mission AI's map. Where is it exactly?"

Elena's response came after a long pause. "Two point three kilometers northeast. At the base of the third escarpment. The Mission AI flagged it as a seismic resonance anomaly. A paleo-channel structure buried at approximately eighty meters."

"Eighty meters," Imani repeated. "That's beyond our current drill string."

"Correct. But it's real. The AI is certain."

"Certain isn't data."

"It's better than data," Elena said. "It's a signal. The planet is telling us where to look. We just have to listen."

Imani closed her eyes. She could feel the weight of the crew's expectations pressing on her. She could feel the hope draining out of the day, replaced by something harder, something more honest.

She opened her eyes and looked at the horizon.

"Tessa," she said. "How long to extend the drill string by twenty meters?"

"We'd need to break down the second crawler's cargo and reconfigure the mounts. Six hours. Maybe seven."

"Then start breaking down."

"You want to go to eighty meters? With the bits we have?"

"We're going to eighty meters with everything we have," Imani said. "Load the crawlers. We're moving to the third escarpment."

The crew looked at her. For a moment, no one moved.

Then Tessa turned and grabbed a cargo strap. The others followed, one by one, pulling on gloves and hoisting equipment.

Gabriel watched them go, then turned to Imani. "You gave them a reason."

"I gave them more work."

"That's the same thing. Work is the only thing that keeps hope alive on Mars. You can't wish your way through this world. You have to drill."

Imani looked at him. "That's a good line. Did you just make it up?"

"Recorded it," Gabriel said. "For the history books."

---

The convoy moved again at 17:45 local time, crawling across the plain toward the third escarpment. The sun was low in the sky, casting long shadows that stretched across the rust-colored ground like black fingers reaching for the crawlers.

Imani drove in silence. The terrain was rough here, buckled by ancient tectonic forces, and the crawler's suspension groaned with every ridge and depression. She kept her eyes on the ground, reading the surface, looking for signs of the paleo-channel that the Mission AI had promised.

Two kilometers. Three. The escarpment grew in her window, a wall of dark rock that rose eighty meters above the plain. Its face was scarred and layered, the striations of a billion years of Martian history written in the strata.

"Mission AI," she said. "Give me the precise coordinates."

A voice came through her helmet speakers—smooth, warm, completely inhuman. "The paleo-channel is beneath your current position. The seismic resonance suggests a buried riverbed, three hundred meters wide, filled with sedimentary deposits and capped by a basalt flow of approximately thirty meters. The ice horizon is at seventy-nine meters."

"Seventy-nine. You're sure."

"I am certain of the resonance signature. I cannot guarantee the composition of the target. But the geological model is consistent with a water-ice lens of significant volume."

"What's your confidence?"

"Eighty-seven percent."

Imani considered that. Eighty-seven percent. That was higher than the Earth-based surveys had been. Higher than anything she'd worked with since landing.

She stopped the crawler and got out.

The ground here was different. Darker. The regolith had a sheen to it, a faint glitter that caught the light. She knelt and touched it, feeling the texture through her glove. Small flakes. Mica, maybe. Or something else.

"Arun. I'm seeing reflective particles in the surface material. Can you analyze?"

A pause. "Spectrometer confirms. Phyllosilicates. Iron-magnesium smectite. These are clay minerals that form in the presence of water over extended periods."

"This was a riverbed."

"This was a river. Billions of years ago. A massive, flowing body of water that carved this channel and deposited these sediments. The clay alone suggests a formation period of at least ten million years."

Imani stood up and looked at the escarpment. The river that had carved it was gone. The water had evaporated, frozen, sublimated, scattered into space. But the evidence remained. The scars were still there, written in the rock.

"Set up the rig," she said. "We're drilling at the base of the escarpment. Aim for seventy-nine meters."

The crew moved. They were tired now, the adrenaline of the first drill fading into the hard reality of the second shift. But they moved. They set the anchors. They mounted the extended string. They ran the diagnostics.

Imani watched from the control station, her eyes fixed on the drill as it touched the surface.

"Starting at 19:02 local time," she said. "Log it."

The bit bit into the ground.

The first twenty meters were fast. Loose fill, fractured rock, the debris of a billion years of erosion. Then the basalt hit, and the grinding started again. Slow. Careful. Meter by meter.

At forty meters, they changed the bit. The crew was faster this time, thirty-five minutes from stop to restart. At sixty meters, they changed again. The second spare. The last one.

At seventy-two meters, the drill hit something different.

The torque reading spiked, then smoothed. The pitch dropped. The machine started making a sound Imani had never heard before—a high, keening whine that cut through the vibration.

"Contact," Tessa said. "Something changed."

"Pull the string," Imani said. "Slow."

It took forty minutes to bring the core up from seventy-two meters. The crew gathered around the extraction tray, their visors fogging from the heat of their breath, their eyes fixed on the barrel as it slid into the light.

The core was white.

Not gray. Not brown. White. Translucent. Solid. It glittered in the Martian sunlight, catching the rays and bending them into fragments of rainbow that scattered across the ground.

Imani stepped forward and touched it. It was cold. Hard. Clean.

Ice.

"Arun," she said. "Analysis."

The pause lasted five seconds. Then Arun's voice, different now. Warmer. "Ninety-eight point seven percent purity. A clean ice lens with minimal sediment inclusion. Estimated volume from the radar signature: seventeen meters thickness, extending at least two hundred meters in all directions."

Imani didn't move. She kept her glove on the ice, feeling its coldness through the suit's insulation.

The crew was cheering. She could hear them through the radio, their voices rising in a chorus of relief and joy that cut through the silence of the Martian plain.

But Imani stayed quiet, her hand on the ice, thinking about what Elena had said. About honesty. About the planet not caring about human timelines.

The ice was here. It had always been here. But it had been hidden behind walls of basalt and clay, buried under the rubble of geological time, guarded by a planet that didn't give up its secrets easily.

"Maps lie," she said, to no one in particular. "But the planet doesn't. You just have to know how to read its scars."

Gabriel's camera was on her. She could feel its lens tracking her, recording the moment for the history books.

She didn't look at it. She kept her eyes on the ice, on the white core that glittered in the dying light, on the promise that had taken them ten hours and a thousand kilometers to fulfill.

The water was here.

Now they just had to bring it home.
